problem_markdown: Let $f$ map positive integers to positive integers and satisfy $f(n+1)>f(f(n))$ for every $n\ge1$. Prove $f(n)=n$ for all $n$.
solutions_markdown:
We prove by induction that $f(k)$ is the unique minimum of $\{f(j):j\ge k\}$. For $k=1$, every $f(j)$ with $j>1$ exceeds the value $f(f(j-1))$, so cannot be a global minimum. A minimum exists among positive integers; therefore it occurs uniquely at one.

Assume the assertion through $k$. The successive tail minima give $f(k)\ge k$. For $j>k+1$, we have $f(j-1)>f(k)\ge k$, so $f(f(j-1))$ belongs to the tail beginning at $k+1$. As $f(j)>f(f(j-1))$, the minimum of that tail cannot occur at $j>k+1$. It therefore occurs uniquely at $k+1$.

Thus $f$ is strictly increasing and $f(n)\ge n$. If $f(n)\ge n+1$, monotonicity would give $f(f(n))\ge f(n+1)$, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence $f(n)=n$.
